key_insight: Machine-learned dynamics reveal that small polarons at reduced rutile TiO2(110) surfaces move orders of magnitude more slowly than in bulk because surface pathways are geometrically constrained and vacancies trap nearby electrons.
engineering_relevance: This explains why porous rutile TiO2 can show much lower electron mobility than single-crystal material, informing defect and surface engineering for photocatalysis, photovoltaics, batteries, and energy storage.
method: Extended a machine-learning-assisted polaron dynamics framework to a redox-active oxide surface.
Ran nanosecond-scale simulations over multiple temperatures on oxygen-deficient rutile TiO2(110).
Mapped polaron trajectories, hopping pathways, and vacancy-induced free-energy effects.
evidence_signal: The study uses several nanoseconds of temperature-dependent dynamics to quantify hopping statistics and show that surface polaron mobility is suppressed by several orders of magnitude relative to bulk.
watch_item: The approach is demonstrated on one representative oxide surface, so transferability to other reducible oxides may require retraining and careful validation.
paper_title: Machine-learned dynamics of surface polarons at reduced oxide surfaces
